items.label: f03-atomic-is-not-everything
items.front: save() writes a temp file and moves it over the target with ATOMIC_MOVE. Name three guarantees this does NOT give.
items.back: No cross-process lock (two app instances can overwrite each other), no compare-and-swap version check on the user's edit, and no guaranteed survival of a power loss (the temp file is never forced to disk).

items.label: f01-validate-in-constructor
items.front: Why does the Expense constructor enforce the invariants (positive id, nonblank title and category, two-place positive amount) instead of only the menu code?
items.back: Records enter from two places: the menu and the saved file. Validating only menu input would leave the file-loading path unprotected, so the rule lives where every Expense is built.

items.label: f04-normalize-fields-not-lines
items.front: What general parsing lesson does the empty-note fix teach?
items.back: Normalization that is fine for recognizing a blank line can destroy structured data. Normalize individual fields by their own contract, not the whole record (in a web app: trimming a signed payload, or turning an empty field into a missing one).

items.label: f02-dual-write
items.front: What is a dual write, and what is the fix the course gives for it?
items.back: One logical change that needs two separate durable writes (for example rows in one file and a next-id counter in another). They can fail independently. The fix is to make it one write: same file under one atomic move, or one database transaction.

choices.text: It is rewritten with only the first record, and the duplicate is dropped
It stays byte for byte the same, as validation throws before a temp file exists

items.explanation: save copies the list and runs it through a fresh ExpenseManager.loadExpenses, which throws on a duplicate id, before createTempFile or any write. The test compares the file bytes after the rejection.

items.prompt: In menu 8 the user types abc where the CLI asks for the expense id. Which line does it print before the menu comes back?

choices.text: Invalid menu option. Please choose a number from 1 to 9.
Could not update expense: For input string: "abc"

Could not update expense: For input string: "abc"

Expense #abc does not exist.

items.explanation: Long.parseLong throws NumberFormatException, a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, so the flow catch prints its message after the prefix. The id text is not trimmed, so " 1" fails the same way. Verified by piping 8 then abc into the CLI.

items.prompt: Before the worked change, an expense saved with an empty note vanished on the next load. What made the loader drop it?

choices.text: toLine left out the note column when it was blank, so five fields were saved
unescape turned the empty note into null, and the constructor refused null
line.trim() removed the trailing tab, so the parser saw five fields
The comment check matched the empty field and skipped the whole line

choices: toLine left out the note column when it was blank, so five fields were saved
unescape turned the empty note into null, and the constructor refused null
line.trim() removed the trailing tab, so the parser saw five fields
The comment check matched the empty field and skipped the whole line

items.explanation: The saved line ends with a tab that introduces the empty sixth field. Trimming the whole line removed it, the parser rejected a five-field record, and the old catch carried on. The fix parses the original line.

items.prompt: In the expense tracker, addExpense receives the amount text "12.300". What does the manager do with it?

choices.text: Rejects it with "Amount must use at most 2 decimal places." for the third digit
Accepts it and stores 12.30, as dropping a trailing zero needs no rounding
Rounds it half-up to 12.30 and prints a warning that a digit was discarded
Accepts it and stores 12.300, as BigDecimal keeps the scale it was parsed with

choices: Rejects it with "Amount must use at most 2 decimal places." for the third digit
Accepts it and stores 12.30, as dropping a trailing zero needs no rounding
Rounds it half-up to 12.30 and prints a warning that a digit was discarded
Accepts it and stores 12.300, as BigDecimal keeps the scale it was parsed with

items.explanation: parseAmount calls setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY); 12.300 -> 12.30 changes no value, so it succeeds. 1.001 would throw and become the precision message.
